qs.q: An infant with a small posterior fossa, misshapen midline cerebellum, downward vermis herniation through the foramen magnum, and a lumbar myelomeningocele is diagnosed with which condition?
qs.e: Chiari Type II malformation is defined by a small posterior fossa, vermis herniation, and almost invariable association with a lumbar myelomeningocele and hydrocephalus. Chiari Type I features low-lying cerebellar tonsils extending into the vertebral canal without a myelomeningocele.
qs.s: CNS Malformations: NTDs, Spina Bifida & Anencephaly Guide: MCQs

qs.q: A research assistant is studying the cerebellum's anatomical and functional divisions. Which cerebellar lobe or division is primarily responsible for balance, equilibrium, and eye movement coordination?
qs.e: The vestibulocerebellum, which corresponds to the flocculonodular lobe, governs balance and eye movement coordination. The anterior lobe primarily coordinates limb movements.

qs.q: Which portion of the cerebellum functions in the planning of sequential movement?
qs.e: The cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) and dentate nucleus are involved in motor planning and coordination of complex, sequential movements. They receive input from cerebral cortex and are important for cognitive aspects of motor control. The other cerebellar regions have different functions related to balance, posture, and limb coordination.

qs.q: The cerebellum receives sensory input from ---
o: All of the mentioned sources above
qs.e: The cerebellum integrates sensory input from the labyrinth, proprioceptors, and the visual system.

qs.q: Climbing fiber input to the cerebellum comes from ---
qs.e: Climbing fibers that project to the cerebellar cortex originate exclusively in the inferior olivary complex.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movement, balance and posture, and contributes to motor learning. Damage produces ataxia, dysmetria and gait instability, which can be life‑threatening if brainstem compression occurs.

sections.p: The cerebellum sits posterior to the brainstem, beneath the occipital lobes. It is divided into two hemispheres and a midline vermis, each with a highly folded cortical mantle (folia).
b: Accounts for ~10% of brain volume but >50% of neurons
Three functional zones: vestibulocerebellum, spinocerebellum, cerebrocerebellum

sections.p: It rests on the dorsal surface of the pons and medulla, anchored by the tentorium cerebelli. The outer cortex contains molecular, Purkinje and granular layers; the deep nuclei lie in the medulla.
b: Vermis controls axial muscles; hemispheres control limb movements
Purkinje cells are the sole output of the cerebellar cortex

sections.p: Anteriorly it contacts the fourth ventricle; posteriorly it is covered by the tentorium. The superior cerebellar peduncles link it to the midbrain, while the middle and inferior peduncles connect to the pons and medulla.
b: Compression of the fourth ventricle → obstructive hydrocephalus
Peduncular injury can produce dysarthria and nystagmus

sections.p: Arterial blood comes from the superior cerebellar artery (SCA), anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) and posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). Venous drainage follows the transverse and sigmoid sinuses.
b: SCA infarct → ipsilateral limb ataxia, dysmetria
AICA infarct may cause facial paralysis and hearing loss

t.b: Which cerebellar artery is occluded? Shows vessel patency; if unavailable, rely on clinical pattern of deficits

sections.p: Cerebellar afferents arrive via mossy and climbing fibers from the spinal cord, vestibular nuclei, pontine nuclei and inferior olive. Efferents exit through the deep nuclei to the thalamus and brainstem.
b: Climbing fibers (inferior olive) provide error signals for motor learning
Mossy fibers convey proprioceptive and vestibular information

sections.p: It fine‑tunes motor output, maintains balance, and stores motor memory. The vestibulocerebellum regulates eye movements; the spinocerebellum monitors limb position; the cerebrocerebellum plans and adapts complex actions.
b: Damage → intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia
Cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome can affect language and executive function

sections.p: Cerebellar lesions present with gait ataxia, dysmetria, nystagmus and dysarthria. Common causes include vascular infarcts, hemorrhage, tumors (pilocytic astrocytoma, medulloblastoma), infections (TB meningitis, neurocysticercosis), and toxic exposures (alcohol, metronidazole).
b: Posterior fossa tumor in children → obstructive hydrocephalus, urgent neurosurgery
Cerebellar stroke in low‑resource settings often linked to hypertension or sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusion

t.b: Result guides surgical vs medical management
Is there infectious meningitis? Elevated protein, low glucose, organisms on stain; if unavailable, treat empirically for TB in endemic areas when clinical suspicion is high

sections.p: Key bedside tests: finger‑nose–finger, heel‑shin, rapid alternating movements, and Romberg. Observe gait, speech and eye movements for cerebellar signs.
b: Intention tremor worsens as target is approached
Dysdiadochokinesia = inability to perform rapid alternating movements

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of severe headache with vomiting and cerebellar signs (possible hemorrhage)
Rapidly worsening gait instability with decreased consciousness (brainstem compression)
New focal cerebellar deficit in a child with vomiting (possible posterior fossa tumor)

faq.q: Why does a cerebellar lesion cause a wide‑based gait?
faq.a: The cerebellum integrates vestibular and proprioceptive input to maintain balance; loss of this coordination forces the patient to widen the base for stability.

faq.q: Can a cerebellar stroke be missed on CT?
faq.a: Early ischemic changes may be subtle; MRI is more sensitive, but a CT that shows hemorrhage or mass effect still warrants urgent action.

faq.q: Is ataxia always due to cerebellar disease?
faq.a: No; sensory ataxia from peripheral neuropathy or proprioceptive loss can mimic cerebellar signs but improves with eyes open (positive Romberg).
